textTitles: The thread that carries the world
Who should pay for the kerb?

paragraphs.text: A plant cannot run away, and everything about its defences follows from that. An animal under attack has options that take seconds; a plant has chemistry, structure and time, and it must solve the problem where it stands. The result is an armoury that is largely invisible to a casual observer and that accounts for a remarkable share of the compounds in the living world, including most of the substances people use as medicines, spices and poisons. A spice rack is, from the plant’s point of view, a shelf of failed deterrents.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The simplest defences are physical and are easy to underestimate. Thorns, spines and hairs deter large animals; a layer of tough fibres makes a leaf expensive to chew; and many grasses take up silica from the soil and deposit it in their leaves, which wears down the teeth of grazing animals over a lifetime. The evolutionary record shows grazers and grasses adjusting to one another over millions of years, with teeth growing higher-crowned as silica content rose. Neither side won, which is the usual outcome of such an arrangement and the reason it lasted.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Chemical defence divides into two strategies with different costs. Some compounds are produced all the time and stored, which is reliable and expensive; others are made only when the plant is attacked, which is cheaper and slower. The second strategy requires the plant to detect damage, and it does so through signals in the wounded tissue: fragments of the plant’s own cell walls, and in several cases molecules from the attacker’s saliva, which allow a plant to respond differently to a caterpillar and to a pair of scissors.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Induced defences spread through the plant faster than a chemical message could travel by diffusion. Electrical signals move along the veins within seconds of a bite, and a leaf far from the wound begins producing defensive compounds before the insect has finished the first leaf. The mechanism has been compared with a nervous system, which annoys plant biologists, because the similarity is in the speed and the routing rather than in anything resembling a brain. The comparison is useful for explaining the speed to a non-specialist and misleading for almost everything else.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Plants also recruit help, and this is where the story becomes strange. A plant attacked by caterpillars releases a mixture of volatile compounds, and the wasps that lay eggs in those caterpillars use the mixture to find them; the plant is, in effect, calling for a predator. The blend differs by attacker, so the signal carries information about which insect is feeding, and neighbouring plants of the same species respond to the same volatiles by preparing their own defences before they are touched. Whether that counts as communication or as eavesdropping is argued about at length, and the plants are indifferent to the distinction.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Everything above has a cost, and the accounting is the part that decides what evolves. A plant that defends heavily grows more slowly, produces fewer seeds and competes badly where herbivores are rare; a plant that defends little does well until the insects arrive. The pattern observed across species follows this logic: fast-growing plants in disturbed ground defend cheaply and replace lost tissue, while slow-growing plants in poor soil, where a leaf is expensive to replace, defend expensively and keep their leaves for years.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Agriculture has removed a great deal of this by accident. Breeding for yield and for taste has selected against bitter compounds, which are usually the defensive ones, and a field of a single variety is an invitation that no wild population presents. Some of the replacement is chemical, applied from a tank; some is a return to the original, with breeders reintroducing defensive traits from wild relatives, and the difficulty there is that the same compounds that deter an insect often make the crop less pleasant to eat.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The practical interest now is in triggering defences rather than adding them. Compounds that switch on a plant’s own induced response can be sprayed, and in trials they reduce damage without killing anything; the plant pays the metabolic cost, so yields fall slightly, which is the trade that has to be judged crop by crop. It is a less dramatic idea than engineering a new toxin, and it works with a system that has been tested by several hundred million years of insects.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The thread that carries the world

paragraphs.text: Almost all intercontinental communication travels through glass. A cable no thicker than a garden hose, lying on the sea floor, carries the traffic of a continent, and there are several hundred such cables in service. Satellites carry a small fraction of the total and are used mainly where a cable cannot go; the popular image of global communication as something that happens in space is almost exactly wrong.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The physics that makes it possible is simple enough to demonstrate with a jug of water. Light travelling inside a medium can be trapped by the boundary with a medium of lower refractive index, and reflects along the inside of a stream of water poured from a jug. A glass fibre does the same with a core and a surrounding layer of slightly different composition; the light entering one end reflects thousands of times along the way and emerges at the other. The trick is old; what was hard was making a fibre in which the light survives the journey.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Turning that demonstration into a cable took a decade of work on purity rather than on optics. Ordinary glass absorbs light so strongly that a signal would fade within metres; the breakthrough came from removing impurities, particularly water, until the glass was transparent enough for a signal to travel kilometres without amplification. The target that engineers set themselves at the time was considered unreachable by most of the field, and it was reached within four years. The story is quoted in engineering schools as an example of a target that was useful precisely because it looked absurd.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Laying the cable is heavy industry with a nineteenth-century flavour. A ship loads thousands of kilometres of cable into tanks, sails a surveyed route, and pays it out over the stern at a speed matched to the depth so that the cable lies flat rather than in loops; near shore it is ploughed into the seabed to protect it from anchors and trawls. Most faults are within twenty kilometres of land, and almost all of them are caused by ships rather than by anything in the deep. Sharks, which appear in every popular account, are responsible for a negligible share.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Repair is a slower business than most users imagine. A fault is located by measuring how long a test pulse takes to return, a repair ship sails to the position, grapples the cable from the sea floor, lifts one end to the surface, splices in a new section and lowers it back; the whole operation takes days in good weather and weeks in bad. There are fewer than sixty such ships in the world, and several of them are decades old. A region with a single repair ship on station is a region where a second fault means waiting.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Capacity has grown in a way that has nothing to do with laying more glass. The same fibre now carries many signals at once, each on a slightly different wavelength, and the electronics at either end have improved so quickly that a cable installed twenty years ago carries many times the traffic it was designed for. Upgrading the ends is cheap compared with laying a cable, which is why the useful life of a route is measured in decades and why the economics reward whoever laid the first one. A route that looked like a gamble in its first year is usually the cheapest capacity on the market by its tenth.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Ownership has shifted in the past decade and the shift is not widely noticed. Cables were historically built by consortia of telephone companies; a large share of new capacity is now owned by a handful of content companies that move their own traffic between their own data centres. The engineering is the same and the commercial logic is different: a consortium sells capacity, while a content company builds to reduce its own costs and has no interest in selling anything.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The concentration is the part worth worrying about. A country served by two cables is a country that can be cut off by two accidents, and several island states are in exactly that position; the same is true of routes that pass through a single narrow sea. Redundancy is expensive and looks wasteful until the day it is needed, which is the oldest problem in infrastructure and is no easier here than anywhere else.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Who should pay for the kerb?

paragraphs.text: The kerb is the most valuable land in a city that nobody prices. A metre of street outside a shop can be a parking space, a loading bay, a cycle lane, a bus stop, a tree, a terrace or a place to put bins, and in most cities the allocation between these uses was settled decades ago by habit rather than by any decision that could be pointed to. The argument about parking is, underneath, an argument about who that land belongs to.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ingrid Sorensen puts the case in terms of price. A parking space in a busy district costs the city something to provide and is given away or sold far below what the space would fetch in any other use, so demand exceeds supply, drivers circle looking for a place, and that circling is itself a substantial share of the traffic in a shopping street. Set the price so that roughly one space in ten is free at any time, she argues, and the circling stops, the loading bays clear and the kerb starts to behave like a resource rather than a queue.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Miguel Duarte agrees about the economics and objects to what is done with the money. Charging for the kerb is a charge on the people who use it, and in many districts those people include tradespeople, carers and shift workers who have no alternative at the hours they travel. A price that is set correctly and a revenue that disappears into a general budget is, in his description, a regressive tax with a clever justification; where the money returns to the street as better pavements, lighting and services, the same charge is defensible and is defended by residents.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Hanne Lauritzen studies what happens to shops. Retailers consistently overestimate the share of their customers who arrive by car, in surveys by a factor of two or more, and consistently oppose changes to parking on the strength of that estimate. Where kerb space has been reallocated and measured afterwards, turnover on the street has usually risen, though not always and not immediately, and the shops that suffer are those that genuinely depend on drivers carrying heavy goods. She regards the gap between the belief and the measurement as the single biggest obstacle to any change.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Oleg Barysh is interested in enforcement rather than in policy. A rule that is not enforced becomes the real rule, he argues, and a city that prices its kerb and then tolerates parking on the pavement has simply moved the free space rather than removed it; the loading bay occupied all day by a private car is the ordinary condition in most places. He notes that enforcement is unpopular, is frequently contracted out, and that contracting it to a company paid per ticket produces exactly the behaviour anybody would predict.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The evidence on what happens to traffic overall is more modest than either side claims. Removing parking from a street does not by itself reduce driving in a city; it changes where cars stop, and the effect on how many journeys are made depends on what is offered instead and on whether the surrounding network absorbs the change. Reviews of many schemes find small reductions where parking policy was part of a package and no reliable effect where it stood alone.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What has changed the practical argument is delivery. A street designed when goods arrived in a weekly lorry now receives dozens of small vans a day, and a city that has no loading provision gets those vans on the pavement, in the cycle lane or on a double yellow line with the hazard lights on. Several cities have responded by converting parking to timed loading bays, which is unpopular with residents in the morning and popular with the same residents by the afternoon, when their own parcel arrives.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The defensible position is that the kerb should be allocated deliberately and reviewed, rather than settled by whoever got there first. That means measuring what the space is used for, pricing it where demand exceeds supply, spending the revenue visibly on the street it came from, enforcing the rules that result, and accepting that the right answer differs between a market street, a residential terrace and a road outside a school. It is an unexciting programme, and the cities that have followed it have quieter streets and fewer arguments than those that have not.
paragraphs.label: H
